explanations.explanation: That's it. Samuel, Israel's prophet, tells them that if they're returning to the LORD with all their hearts, the foreign gods and Ashtoreths have to go (1 Samuel 7:3). Notice he says ALL their hearts, not a nice chunk of them. Half a heart is like half a batch of dough: nothing you'd want to bake. Then verse 4 says they put away the Baals and Ashtoreths.

explanations.answer: The weapons of their fighting men
explanations.explanation: Samuel never asks anyone to hand in a sword here. His request is about what they worship: the foreign gods and Ashtoreths. He also tells them to prepare their hearts for the LORD and serve Him only. This is a heart matter, friend, not an armory matter.

explanations.answer: The gold from the guilt offering
explanations.explanation: No gold shows up anywhere in Samuel's request. What he names is the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among them. He wants them to serve the LORD only (1 Samuel 7:3). If it's another god, it goes. That's the whole list.

You've got it, baker. Samuel says, “…prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only.” (1 Samuel 7:3) Think of it like warming the oven before the dough goes in. The getting ready comes first, and then the serving.

It's actually in there, friend. Samuel tells them, “…prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only.” (1 Samuel 7:3) It sits right between putting away the foreign gods and serving the LORD alone. Easy to skate past it when you're reading fast.

Philistines is right. Samuel says that if they do these things, the LORD “will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:3) That's the promise on the table. And remember, it comes after the putting away and the serving, not before.

The Egyptians never come up in this passage. Samuel's promise is about the hand of the Philistines. They're the ones who show up marching later in the chapter (1 Samuel 7:7). Wrong people, right idea of a promise.

The Moabites aren't in this story at all. Samuel says the LORD will deliver them from the hand of the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:3). And sure enough, the Philistine rulers are the ones who march up. Samuel knew exactly who was coming.

explanations.answer: Pray to the LORD on their behalf
explanations.explanation: Yes. Samuel says, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf.” (1 Samuel 7:5) He doesn't say he'll fight or negotiate. He says he'll pray. That's a prophet who knows where to take a problem.

explanations.answer: Lead them out against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Not yet, baker. Samuel's offer is to pray to the LORD on their behalf (1 Samuel 7:5). The charge out of Mizpah doesn't happen until after the LORD has thundered, and the men of Israel are the ones who do the charging (1 Samuel 7:10-11). Samuel's job at this point is prayer.

explanations.answer: Bring the ark of the LORD there
explanations.explanation: The ark stays put. Verse 2 says it remained at Kiriath-jearim, and nobody moves it in this passage. Samuel's promise at Mizpah is that he will pray to the LORD on their behalf (1 Samuel 7:5). No hauling required.

Sinned is the word. At Mizpah they fast and confess, “We have sinned against the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:6) Saying it out loud is the hard part, friend. I'd rather admit I burned a batch than admit that. They said the true thing plainly.

The fighting hasn't started yet. What they confess at Mizpah is, “We have sinned against the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:6) The Philistines don't even march up until the next verse. First comes the confession.

They did say something, but "spoken" isn't the word. The people confess, “We have sinned against the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:6) It's about what they've done, not what they've said. And they confess it while fasting.

You've got it. The text says Samuel “judged the Israelites at Mizpah.” (1 Samuel 7:6) Judging is Samuel's ongoing work, and verse 15 says he does it all the days of his life. Mizpah is just one stop on that road.

The text says it plainly: Samuel “judged the Israelites at Mizpah.” (1 Samuel 7:6) He's right there with the gathered people. Judging is his work, and verse 15 says he keeps doing it all the days of his life.

The text says the opposite, friend. When the Israelites learn the Philistines are coming, “they feared the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:7) I think that's very human. A gathering full of confession, and then a march of rulers heading your way. Fear makes sense.

That's right. The text says the Israelites “feared the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:7) And notice what they do with that fear. They go straight to Samuel and ask him to keep crying out to the LORD (1 Samuel 7:8).

explanations.answer: Keep crying out to the LORD for them
explanations.explanation: Yes. They say to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.” (1 Samuel 7:8) Afraid, they ask for prayer. If a worried baker ever wonders where to take it first, this is a good example.

explanations.answer: Make peace with the Philistine rulers
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks for a treaty. The Israelites say, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us.” (1 Samuel 7:8) They want the LORD to save them from the hand of the Philistines. No peace talks appear in this scene.

explanations.answer: Carry the ark out into the battle
explanations.explanation: The ark isn't part of this scene. Verse 2 says it remained at Kiriath-jearim. What the Israelites ask of Samuel is, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us.” (1 Samuel 7:8) It's a request for prayer, not a parade.

explanations.answer: He thunders loudly against the Philistines
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Verse 10 says the LORD “thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel.” Samuel was still offering the burnt offering when it happened. Israel didn't have to swing first.

explanations.answer: He tells Israel to make peace with them
explanations.explanation: No such message comes. The text says the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines that day (1 Samuel 7:10). The Philistines flee, and Israel pursues. Peace talks never get a seat at this table.

explanations.answer: He tells Samuel to stop the offering
explanations.explanation: Samuel never gets told to stop. The text says that as the Philistines drew near, Samuel was offering up the burnt offering. Right then, the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:10). The offering and the answer happen together.

That's not how it goes, friend. The LORD thundered loudly and threw the Philistines into such confusion “that they fled before Israel.” (1 Samuel 7:10) They don't hold their ground at all. They run, and the men of Israel chase them (1 Samuel 7:11).

Right. The Philistines don't last. The LORD thundered against them and threw them into confusion, and they fled before Israel (1 Samuel 7:10). Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued them (1 Samuel 7:11). That's a short fight, baker.
Ebenezer is right. Samuel sets up the stone between Mizpah and Shen and names it Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:12). A stone is hard to argue with. Every time someone passes it, there it sits, reminding them.

Galeed is a real stone name, but it belongs to another story. Jacob, Isaac's son, called a heap of stones Galeed (Genesis 31:47). Samuel's stone here is named Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:12). Different stone, different man, different moment.

Peniel is a name from a different story. Jacob, Isaac's son, named a place Peniel (Genesis 32:30). Samuel's stone between Mizpah and Shen is named Ebenezer (1 Samuel 7:12). Good memory on the other name, though.

Helped is the word. Samuel names the stone Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12) It's a simple sentence, and it looks back over everything that's just happened. A stone that says thank you.
Not "tested." Samuel says, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12) That's what the name Ebenezer is attached to. It points to the help they just saw at Mizpah.

Close in sound to a lot of Bible words, but not this one. Samuel says, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” (1 Samuel 7:12) Nothing about a warning here. The stone is there to say the LORD has helped them.

You've got it, baker. The text says the cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel (1 Samuel 7:14). Israel also delivered the surrounding territory from the hand of the Philistines. A whole stretch of land comes back.

The text says the opposite. The cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel (1 Samuel 7:14). The surrounding territory was delivered from the hand of the Philistines too. It all comes back.
The Amorites, that's right. The text says, “And there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites.” (1 Samuel 7:14) Land restored, and peace on another side too. That's a good stretch of days.

The Moabites don't appear in this passage. The peace in verse 14 is between the Israelites and the Amorites. The same verse says the cities from Ekron to Gath were restored to Israel. Good guess on a neighbor, but not the one named.

The Edomites aren't mentioned here. The text says there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites (1 Samuel 7:14). It comes right after the cities and territory return to Israel. Try the Amorites next time.

Simple as that. The text says Samuel would return to Ramah “because his home was there.” (1 Samuel 7:17) After all that traveling, he goes home. I get that, friend. Even a man with a big route wants his own bed at the end of it.

explanations.answer: Because the ark is kept there
explanations.explanation: The ark isn't in Ramah. Verse 2 says it remained at Kiriath-jearim. The reason the text gives for Ramah is that Samuel's home was there (1 Samuel 7:17).

explanations.answer: Because the people asked him to
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anyone asked. It gives the reason itself: Samuel returned to Ramah “because his home was there.” (1 Samuel 7:17) No request, no summons. He just goes home.
An altar, yes. The text says that in Ramah Samuel judged Israel “and built an altar to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 7:17) Even at home, he builds a place to worship. That's how this passage closes.
No temple here, baker. Samuel builds an altar to the LORD in Ramah (1 Samuel 7:17). A temple doesn't come up anywhere in this passage. This one's a smaller thing, built at his home.

No towers in this passage. In Ramah, Samuel judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD (1 Samuel 7:17). The only thing he sets up standing earlier is the Ebenezer stone. The last thing he builds is the altar.
